L'AQUILA, Italy (CNN) -- The youngest hadn't lived half a year. The oldest had lived nearly a hundred. A rescue worker Friday kisses the coffin of a child killed by this week's earthquake in central Italy. The official government list of victims from this week's earthquake in central Italy reached 287 on Friday, as Italians held a mass state funeral to lay the victims to rest. They included Antonio Loavan Ghiroceanu, who was born December 11. He would have been  6 months old on Saturday. The oldest-known victim of the quake was Evandro Testa, 96, who was born in 1913. More than 200 caskets were lined up at the funeral, draped with flowers. At least one small white coffin belonging to a child sat atop a larger coffin, a baby's pastel outfit hanging off the side. The funeral was being held outside a hangar in Coppito, a town adjacent to the earthquake's epicenter of L'Aquila. Officials elected to hold the Mass in the open air to avoid the risk of injury from falling debris. Aftershocks continue to shake the region more than four days after the earthquake, and some were even felt during Friday's funeral. All of the area's cardinals and bishops, along with 100 priests, attended the special funeral Mass. Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was also there, greeting and embracing some of the thousands of mourners before the service. Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone presided over the Mass as an envoy from Pope Benedict XVI, who plans to visit the region after Easter.  Watch Italy bury its dead » . Bertone said the funeral was a "precious moment" to understand the meaning of life and death. "Everything can stop in a second -- projects, plans -- everything finishes. All that remains is love," he said. Watch more on funeral . Mourners, who were transported to the funeral on buses, dabbed their eyes and noses. Some stared at the ground or held each other. Few appeared focused on anything but remembering the victims. "I feel rebirth in the heart, because below that rubble there is a will to rebuild, to start again, to plan and to dream," Bertone said, offering a message of hope. The towns of L'Aquila and the surrounding region, he said, "will come back stronger, will have more courage and give life to these places with that power and strength and dignity of the soul that distinguishes them." As well as sending Bertone to deliver his message, the pope sent holy oils to L'Aquila and a chalice with which to take Communion. Archbishop Giuseppe Molinari of L'Aquila also planned to deliver a message. The 6.3-magnitude quake Monday morning left about 30,000 people without their homes. Almost 20,000 of them are braving chilly nights in tents while about 11,000 others are staying in hotels, said Agostino Miozzo, a spokesman for the Italian Civil Protection Agency. Watch more on the aftermath . Recovering from such losses and rebuilding the city of L'Aquila will take several years, according to Miozzo. The medieval city is about 120 km (75 miles) northeast of Rome. Berlusconi has said rebuilding will cost several billion euros. Aftershocks have heightened anxiety in the area -- including a moderate 5.6 magnitude tremor that struck the area Tuesday. "The mood is a little bit afraid," said Marco Volponi of the Civil Protection agency. He was working in a tent camp, housing people whose homes were inhabitable. In the nearby village of Onna, 40 people -- more than one out of every eight residents in the town of 300 -- were killed in the earthquake. On some streets, every single home was destroyed. Anna Rita Difilice lost her son, Fabio, 20, to the quake -- the deadliest to strike Italy in decades and the first major quake in the country in seven years. She said she doesn't know what comes next for her. Her village has become populated with tents, fold-up beds and feeding stations handing out food, water and other supplies for survivors. But she said she knew one thing: she's not going anywhere. "My son died here," she said. "There is no way I'm leaving this town -- not ever."

Nestled at the foot of the snow-capped Gran Sasso mountains in the rugged Abruzzo region, **L'Aquila** has long been one of **Italy**’s most captivating historic cities. With its labyrinthine medieval streets, striking Renaissance palaces, and vibrant university culture, it embodies the timeless charm of central Italy. Yet, for much of the international community, the city’s name became indelibly linked to a single, tragic moment in modern history.

In the early morning hours of April 6, 2009, a devastating magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck the region. Within seconds, centuries of architectural heritage were reduced to rubble, hundreds of lives were lost, and tens of thousands were left homeless. As emergency responders rushed to the scene, international news organizations scrambled to cover the disaster. **CNN** was among the major global networks that brought the heartbreaking images of L'Aquila into living rooms around the world. Broadcasts showed terrifying footage of collapsed basilicas, frantic search-and-rescue operations, and thousands of residents seeking shelter in tent cities. Through CNN's continuous coverage, the world watched a community mourn, but also witnessed the early sparks of an incredible human resolve.

In the years following the disaster, the narrative surrounding L'Aquila gradually began to transform. The path to recovery was long, complex, and often fraught with political and logistical hurdles. Yet, stone by stone, the people of L'Aquila worked to reclaim their city. The majestic Basilica of Santa Maria di Collemaggio—whose severe damage was once a central image in CNN’s post-quake reporting—was meticulously restored, eventually winning prestigious European heritage awards for its reconstruction.

Today, global media outlets like **CNN** cover L'Aquila through a very different lens. Rather than being defined solely by tragedy, the city is increasingly highlighted as a symbol of profound resilience and a top destination for travelers looking to experience authentic **Italy** off the beaten path. Visitors are returning to sample local delicacies like saffron-infused dishes and Arrosticini, explore the nearby Apennine hiking trails, and admire the seamlessly restored Baroque and Gothic facades.

L'Aquila’s journey from catastrophic destruction to a quiet cultural rebirth serves as a powerful reminder of the Italian spirit. It stands today not as a monument to what was lost, but as a living testament to the endurance of community, art, and history—a story that continues to inspire audiences worldwide.

**By CNN Staff**
Updated 4:15 PM EDT, Friday, April 10, 2009

**L'AQUILA, Italy (CNN) —** Under a grey, overcast sky on Good Friday, a grieving nation stood still as Italy held an agonizing mass state funeral for the victims of the devastating earthquake that shattered the historic region of Abruzzo earlier this week.

Over 200 coffins, arranged in neat, heartbreaking rows, covered the vast asphalt parade ground of the Guardia di Finanza military academy on the outskirts of L'Aquila. Atop the larger mahogany caskets lay smaller, white coffins—some adorned with stuffed animals, teddy bears, and handwritten notes from classmates—marking the dozens of children killed when the magnitude 6.3 quake struck in the early morning hours of Monday.

As incense drifted over the sea of mourners, sob-racked silence was broken only by the sound of wind and the distant rumble of minor aftershocks that continue to rattle the region.

### A nation in mourning

The Italian government declared Friday a national day of mourning, flying flags at half-staff across the country. Businesses closed, and television networks muted their usual programming to broadcast the solemn ceremony live.

The Catholic Church granted a special dispensation to hold a funeral Mass on Good Friday—the only day of the liturgical calendar when Mass is traditionally not celebrated—underscoring the profound scale of the tragedy.

Leading the service, Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone delivered a message of solace to a crowd of thousands, which included weeping relatives, emergency responders in dust-covered uniforms, and the nation's top political leaders.

"There is no shame in tears," Cardinal Bertone told the congregation. "Together, we have lived through the agony of shattered homes, of lives torn away in a matter of seconds. Yet, our faith reminds us that life does not end beneath the rubble."

Cardinal Bertone also read a personal message from Pope Benedict XVI, who expressed his "deep spiritual closeness" to the victims and promised to visit the devastated area soon. 

"In these dramatic hours when a whole region is weeping for its dead, I am with you," the Pope’s message read. "The Pope feels your grief."

### 'We will not abandon you'

Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, visible moved, moved through the crowds before and after the two-hour service, embracing weeping relatives and shaking the hands of tired rescue workers.

"Today is a day for tears and prayer," Berlusconi told reporters following the service. "Tomorrow will be a day for relentless work. I say to the people of Abruzzo: We will not abandon you. We will rebuild everything, and we will give you back your homes."

Berlusconi’s government has promised millions of euros in emergency aid and pledged to construct new towns for those displaced before the harsh winter sets in later this year. 

However, political promises offered little immediate comfort to those sitting on plastic chairs beside the caskets of their loved ones.

### Stories of survival and profound loss

For the survivors, the funeral was a crushing realization of the human cost of the disaster.

Pierluigi Rossi, 42, sat head in hands beside a tiny white casket holding his 8-year-old daughter, Sofia. He had spent hours digging through the debris of their home with his bare hands on Monday morning, only to find her too late.

"I lost my mother, my home, and my little girl in five seconds," Rossi whispered, his hands trembling as he stroked the polished wood of the coffin. "I don’t care about rebuilding houses. I don't care about the money. How do you rebuild a life when your heart has been pulled out of your chest?"

A few rows away stood Maria Cantalini, 65, who lost three neighbors when her apartment building collapsed in downtown L'Aquila. She currently lives in one of the sprawling tent cities set up on the outskirts of the city.

"We are alive, but our souls are buried back there in the historic center," Cantalini said, wiping away tears with a handkerchief. "L'Aquila was a vibrant city of students, art, and history. Now it feels like a graveyard. But seeing all of Italy standing with us today... it gives us a small reason to keep breathing."

### The staggering toll

As rescue crews begin to wind down the search for survivors, the sheer scale of the catastrophe has become starkly clear. 

According to Italian civil protection officials, the latest casualty statistics paint a grim picture:
* **Death Toll:** At least 289 people confirmed dead, with several still missing.
* **Injured:** More than 1,500 people, dozens of whom remain in critical condition in regional hospitals.
* **Displaced:** An estimated 66,000 people left homeless, with roughly 35,000 staying in temporary tent camps and another 20,000 sheltered in hotels along the Adriatic coast.
* **Aftershocks:** Over 1,000 tremors recorded since Monday's main quake, continuing to destabilize fragile structures.

As the funeral service concluded, rescue workers gently lifted the coffins one by one into waiting hearses to be taken for private burials across the region. With each hearse that pulled away, the crowd erupted into rhythmic, respectful applause—a traditional Italian gesture of tribute and final farewell.

For the people of L'Aquila, the long, painful road to recovery has only just begun.

**A NATION IN MOURNING: ITALY BIDS FAREWELL TO EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS IN SOLEMN STATE FUNERAL**

**L’AQUILA, Italy — April 10, 2009** — Against a stark backdrop of concrete and mountain mist, a devastated nation gathered today to mourn the victims of Italy’s worst natural disaster in nearly three decades. 

Under a papal dispensation on Good Friday—the one day in the Roman Catholic calendar when Mass is traditionally not celebrated—a mass state funeral was held in the central Italian city of L’Aquila. The tearful ceremony honored the more than 200 victims killed when a magnitude 6.3 earthquake shattered the Abruzzo region in the early hours of Monday morning.

### A Sea of Coffins

The service took place on the concrete parade grounds of the Guardia di Finanza (Finance Police) academy on the outskirts of L’Aquila—one of the few structures large enough and structurally sound enough to hold the thousands of mourners. 

Arranged in four long, heartbreaking rows were 205 wooden coffins. Resting atop the adult caskets were spring flowers, framed photographs, and personal mementos. Most harrowing, however, were the small, white coffins of children and infants scattered among the adult caskets. On top of these lay soft toys, teddy bears, and drawings from classmates—a poignant reminder of the young lives cut short.

An estimated 1,600 grieving family members sat among the rows of caskets, clutching one another as rescue workers, soldiers, and volunteers stood vigil. Thousands more gathered outside the gates, while millions across Italy watched the live broadcast in silent solidarity as the country observed an official National Day of Mourning.

### Words of Solace on Good Friday

The Mass was celebrated by the Vatican’s Secretary of State, Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone, alongside L’Aquila’s Archbishop, Giuseppe Molinari. Because Catholic doctrine forbids the celebration of the Eucharist on Good Friday, Pope Benedict XVI granted a special dispensation for the mass to take place.

In his homily, Cardinal Bertone addressed the profound grief hanging over the region, offering a message of hope amid catastrophe. 

"There is a pain that cannot be explained, a sorrow that leaves us speechless," Bertone told the crowd. "Yet, even in the darkness of tragedy, life does not end here. We must look forward with the strength of faith and community."

A personal message from Pope Benedict XVI was also read to the crowd, in which the Pontiff assured the survivors that he was "spiritually present" with them and expressed his deep sorrow for the loss of life, particularly the children. (The Pope is scheduled to visit the disaster zone in the coming days).

In an embrace of religious unity, a short Islamic funeral service was held immediately following the Catholic Mass for the Muslim victims of the quake, conducted by a local imam. 

### Political Unity and National Solidarity

The funeral brought together Italy’s highest political leadership, temporarily setting aside the country’s intense political divisions. President Giorgio Napolitano and Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi stood side by side, visible emotion on their faces as they embraced grieving relatives before and after the service. 

As the names of the victims were read aloud—a agonizing process that took nearly 20 minutes—family members wept openly, leaning over the coffins to kiss the polished wood. 

When the ceremony concluded, members of the *Vigili del Fuoco* (firefighters) and civil protection workers carried the coffins to awaiting hearses. The crowd erupted into a long, sustained round of applause—a traditional Italian gesture of respect for both the deceased and the rescue crews who worked tirelessly through the rubble in the days following the quake.

### The Road Ahead

While today offered a moment of collective grieving, the emergency in Abruzzo remains acute. As of Friday, the official death toll had risen to 289, with search efforts gradually shifting from rescue to recovery.
